sources.title: Fritz Rohrlich, The Dynamics of a Charged Particle, arXiv:0804.4614 (complete 11-page full-text paper)
sources.locator: Sections 1–2, PDF pp. 2–6: finite-size and slowly varying-force conditions, the nonrelativistic Abraham–Lorentz equation, and first-order reduction; the nonrelativistic illustration begins in §3, PDF pp. 6–7. The complete paper was retrieved; these relevant sections were read in full.

contents.name: Sections 1–2: prescribed-force nonrelativistic equation and SI coefficient
contents.support: The article states the nonrelativistic third-order equation and a force-variation condition tied to its time scale. Its Gaussian-unit coefficient is converted to SI as tau=q^2/(6 pi epsilon_0 m c^3). The item adopts this as a restricted effective postulate; the article's broader claim of physical correctness is not adopted.

contents.name: Sections 1–2: runaway and selected nonrelativistic branches
contents.support: The article identifies exponential runaway and future-dependent acceleration as properties of the nonrelativistic equation. The item independently proves the complete solution family, uniqueness of the bounded-future branch, and the smooth pre-force example.

contents.name: Section 2: first-order reduction under a slow-force restriction
contents.support: The paper gives the first-order reduced equation and explains the small-time-scale premise qualitatively. It does not supply the exact residual or uniform second-derivative error bound; the item proves both from the future kernel.

contents.name: Section 1: force-free runaway branch
contents.support: The paper identifies the exponential force-free runaway. The example verifies its acceleration and integrates twice while preserving fixed position and velocity at the chosen initial time.

contents.name: Section 2: harmonic response regime
contents.support: The source's slow-force condition motivates the frequency-scale comparison. The exact phasor and tolerance criterion are derived locally; no source measurement or universal empirical cutoff is asserted.

sources.title: Jack Vanderlinde, Classical Electromagnetic Theory, Fundamental Theories of Physics, Springer (2004), complete 426-page book PDF
sources.locator: Chapter 12, §§12.3–12.4, printed pp. 335–339 (PDF pp. 342–346). The complete 426-page book was retrieved; the direct rigid-sphere calculation, equation of motion, and future-boundary discussion were inspected in full.

contents.name: Section 12.3: rigid-sphere calculation of the Abraham–Lorentz coefficient
contents.support: The book derives the coefficient from retarded fields of a rigid charged sphere and explicitly notes that this rigid extended body is inconsistent with special relativity. This derivation is source context only: the item adopts a separate effective equation and does not claim the singular Maxwell self-field is defined on its own support.

contents.name: Section 12.4: mass-renormalized ODE and future-boundary branch
contents.support: Equations (12–38)–(12–41) display the mass-renormalized Abraham–Lorentz equation, its exponential homogeneous solution, and the future-weighted branch. The item independently checks convergence, differentiates the kernel, proves uniqueness, and constructs preacceleration.

contents.name: Sections 12.3–12.4: equation coefficient and averaging discussion
contents.support: The book supplies the coefficient and discusses averaging, but does not establish the item's exact residual or uniform error bound. Those estimates are derived locally with explicit endpoint control.

contents.name: Section 12.4: force-free homogeneous runaway
contents.support: The homogeneous solution in equation (12–38) agrees with the constructed acceleration branch. The item separately integrates the acceleration and verifies the same position and velocity at the initial time.

contents.name: Section 12.4 and problem 12-2: harmonic-oscillator context
contents.support: The book points to a harmonic-oscillator application of the future-averaged equation. It does not state the phasor error criterion; the item proves the exact amplitude and tolerance condition directly.
